request.prompt: You are grading a TTool AVATAR Block Diagram using the same style of expert human grading described in the TTool-AI paper. Return all scores normalized to the range 0.0 to 1.0, where 1.0 corresponds to 100/100. Review only the block diagram, not the internal state-machine behavior. Focus on: adequacy of the architecture to the specification, whether the chosen blocks capture the required system actors or subsystems, whether exchanges between blocks are reasonable and sufficient, readability, naming consistency, reasonableness of the number of blocks, and declared attributes or interfaces that look pointless, inconsistent, or unsupported. Use the full score range. A model with major missing participants or implausible communication should score low, even if it looks tidy. A model with a coherent decomposition and sensible exchanges should receive high credit even if its decomposition differs from another valid design.
request.input_text:
When a dangerous situation occurs that forces the driver, or the car itself, to perform a
manoeuvre, this can endanger other vehicles. In order to warn other vehicles, the car sends
out a warning message. Nearby cars that are in danger can then react according to the
information provided within the message.
An ECU of the chassis & safety domain detects a danger; this may be the trigger of an airbag,
an obstacle in direction of travel seen by an environmental sensor, or an emergency braking
performed by the driver or an automatic system. The Chassis Safety Controller (CSC) gets
information about the dangerous situation via the Chassis Domain Bus. The CSC will assess
the situation and will take measures to mitigate the danger for the car. The measures will
result in commands to actuator ECUs in the chassis & safety domain and additionally com-
mands to the powertrain domain to get a helpful driving power adjustment. In parallel it
will also send information to the Communication Unit (CU). This information will contain
data about the current vehicle dynamic status and detailed information about the planned
actions (deceleration or acceleration, steering, etc.).
The CU will send out a warning message that contains this information via the DSRC interface to nearby vehicles. The emergency message contains longitude, latitude, altitude,
speed, acceleration and heading of the car, the time of message generation, the expiry time
of the message, an indicator for the reliability of the information, a code that is classifying
the car, an id that is identifying the sender of the message, an event code that is classifying
the emergency situation and the planed acceleration and heading. All this information is
packed in a message frame that adds checksum, information for protocol processing and if
necessary security information.

Functional requirements
- No warning message without a real danger is allowed
- No failure in any single unit may be succeeded by a false message
- No failure of any single communication may be succeeded by a false message
- Any single fault in an ECU has to be detectable
- Information about dangerous events has to be broadcast according to the communica-
tion congestion control algorithms
- Information about the dangers have to be broadcast to other cars with highest priority
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed
Technical Requirements
- The maximum delay from danger detection to broadcast of the car2X message should
be less than 150 ms
- Additional security information on the busses in the chassis and safety & powertrain
domains should be less than 15% of the net data
Security aspects
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed

Use between 4 and 10 blocks

review_result.overall_reason_text: The model captures some core architectural actors of the warning pipeline such as ECU, CSC, CommunicationUnit, PowertrainDomain, ActuatorECU, and DSRCInterface. However, several exchanges contradict the described architecture, important requirements around fault handling, privacy, congestion control, and timing are not meaningfully represented, and the decomposition is inflated with unsupported blocks and attributes. The diagram is therefore parseable but only partially adequate to the specification.

dimension_results.title: Notation and Syntax
dimension_results.reason_text: As a block-level AVATAR-style artifact, it is structurally well formed: blocks, attributes, signals, and resolved exchanges are present, and there are no unresolved exchanges reported. It loses some credit because the model quality is muddied by duplicated auto-suffixed signals and unusual data-as-block constructs, which are hard to justify as disciplined block-diagram notation.

dimension_results.title: Semantic Completeness
dimension_results.reason_text: The core chain from danger detection to broadcast is partly represented, and the message content fields are extensively listed. But major requirement-driven concerns are absent at architectural level: nearby receiving vehicles, single-fault detectability and false-message prevention, congestion-control broadcasting, highest-priority handling, and timing/security-budget constraints are not captured by supported structure or interfaces.

evidence.snippet: Requirements include no false message after single unit/communication failure, ECU fault detectability, congestion control, highest priority broadcast, privacy, and <150 ms delay.
evidence.explanation: These are explicit evaluation targets that should be reflected by the architecture or its declared interfaces.

evidence.snippet: Blocks include ECU, ChassisSafetyController, CommunicationUnit, DSRCInterface, PowertrainDomain, ActuatorECU, but no nearby vehicle / receiver block and no fault-monitoring or congestion-control component.
evidence.explanation: This shows partial architectural coverage with several important participants or mechanisms missing.

issues.element_text: Nearby cars that are in danger can react to the warning message
issues.reason_text: No receiving-car actor or subsystem is modeled.

issues.element_text: Single-fault false-message prevention, detectability, congestion control, highest priority, privacy, timing
issues.reason_text: These major nonfunctional and safety requirements lack concrete architectural realization.

dimension_results.title: Behavioral Consistency
dimension_results.reason_text: The intended information flow is not preserved well. The specification says the CSC receives danger information via the Chassis Domain Bus, assesses it, then sends commands to actuator/powertrain and information to the CU; instead, the model also sends raw dangerDetected directly from ECU to CommunicationUnit, ActuatorECU, and PowertrainDomain, which weakens the intended control logic and safety gating. The DSRC side is also modeled oddly as broadcasting to Car, EmergencyMessage, and MessageFrame blocks rather than clearly to other vehicles via an interface.

evidence.snippet: "The CSC gets information ... via the Chassis Domain Bus" and after assessment sends commands to actuator ECUs, powertrain, and in parallel information to the Communication Unit.
evidence.explanation: This defines the required architectural trigger-condition-effect chain to preserve.

evidence.snippet: ECU sends dangerDetected directly to CommunicationUnit, ActuatorECU, and PowertrainDomain; ChassisDomainBus has no signals; DSRCInterface sends warningMessageSent() to Car, EmergencyMessage, and MessageFrame.
evidence.explanation: These exchanges conflict with the specified mediated flow and produce implausible communication paths.

issues.reason_text: The required bus-mediated transfer to CSC is not actually modeled.

issues.element_text: Direct ECU outputs to CU, ActuatorECU, PowertrainDomain
issues.reason_text: These bypass the specified CSC assessment stage and are behaviorally unsupported.

dimension_results.title: Requirement Traceability
dimension_results.reason_text: Some major requirements can be mapped to model elements, especially the ECU→CSC→CU→DSRC communication chain and message content fields such as location, speed, heading, reliability, senderId, and eventCode. However, several blocks and attributes are unsupported by the requirements, and important requirements cannot be traced to concrete architectural means, so traceability is only partial.

evidence.snippet: Message-related blocks and attributes include longitude, latitude, speed, acceleration, heading, generationTime, expiryTime, reliability, senderId, eventCode, plannedAcceleration, plannedHeading.
evidence.explanation: This gives traceable support for the required emergency message contents.

evidence.snippet: Driver has attributes name/age/gender/license/experience; Car has vin/make/model/year/mileage/color/licensePlate.
evidence.explanation: These structures are not required by the problem and dilute requirement-to-model mapping.

issues.reason_text: The specification mentions driver-triggered manoeuvres, not a personal-data actor with these attributes.
Vehicle identity and consumer-style metadata are unsupported and do not realize stated safety/communication requirements.

dimension_results.title: Pragmatic Clarity
dimension_results.reason_text: The diagram is harder to review than necessary because it exceeds the requested block count, mixes subsystem blocks with data-holder blocks, duplicates message concepts, and contains many pointless attributes. Naming is inconsistent due to generated suffixes on signals, and the overall decomposition looks inflated rather than disciplined.

evidence.explanation: This is an explicit modeling constraint affecting pragmatic quality.
The model exceeds the requested size and carries a large amount of unsupported detail, hurting readability and maintainability.

issues.reason_text: The architecture is over-decomposed relative to the stated constraint.
This duplication obscures the architecture and suggests unnecessary inflation of data concepts into blocks.
